clinicalPearls: Spondyloarthritis (SpA) is a family of immune-mediated inflammatory arthritides sharing clinical, genetic, and pathologic features; classified by ASAS (2009) into axial (axSpA) and peripheral (pSpA). Axial skeletal involvement is hinted at in the name but is NOT mandatory (Harrison 22e p.2879).

axSpA is subdivided into radiographic (r-axSpA, = ankylosing spondylitis [AS]) and nonradiographic (nr-axSpA), the difference based on presence/absence of definitive sacroiliitis on plain radiographs; the two share the same clinical features and disease burden (Harrison 22e p.2880, 2883).

pSpA encompasses psoriatic arthritis (PsA), reactive arthritis (ReA), IBD-associated arthritis, and undifferentiated pSpA; SAPHO, acne-associated, and hidradenitis suppurativa-associated arthritis are sometimes included (Harrison 22e p.2880).
HLA-B27 is the strongest genetic risk factor: present in 85-90% of r-axSpA and 50-90% of nr-axSpA, versus ~5% of the healthy Caucasian population (Harrison 22e p.2881).

Inflammatory back pain (IBP): insidious onset, age <45, chronic (>3 months), improves with exercise/activity but NOT with rest, worse in second half of night with improvement after getting up, and prolonged (>30 min) morning stiffness; this distinguishes it from mechanical back pain (Harrison 22e p.2883).

Characteristic SpA pattern is asymmetric mono-/oligoarticular (<=4 joints) inflammatory arthritis of large lower-limb joints (usually knee) with enthesitis, tendonitis, and dactylitis (sausage digits), contrasting with the symmetric polyarticular MCP/PIP involvement of rheumatoid arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2879).
Hips are the most common nonspinal ('root') joints affected in axSpA; peripheral arthritis occurs in ~30-40% of axSpA patients (Harrison 22e p.2883).

Uveitis is the most common extramusculoskeletal manifestation (~40% of axSpA), typically acute, anterior, unilateral, and episodic; other extra-articular features include psoriasis (~10%) and IBD (frank IBD ~10%, subclinical gut inflammation up to 50%) (Harrison 22e p.2883-2884).

Enthesitis (inflammation at tendon/ligament insertions) is common in axSpA, presenting as heel pain (plantar fasciitis, Achilles insertion), chest wall pain, epicondylitis, or pelvic rim pain; dactylitis is relatively rare in axSpA but common in PsA (Harrison 22e p.2883).

Persistent axial inflammation leads to bony fusion of sacroiliac and apophyseal joints and syndesmophyte formation; complete ankylosis of the spine is termed 'bamboo spine,' seen in only a very small percentage of late-stage AS patients (Harrison 22e p.2880, 2884).

Typical SpA syndesmophytes are vertically oriented, distinguishing them from the horizontal osteophytes of spinal osteoarthritis; PsA syndesmophytes are often chunky and nonmarginal (Harrison 22e p.2884, 2889).

Reactive arthritis follows infectious gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or genitourinary Chlamydia; classic features include urethritis, conjunctivitis, mucosal ulcers, and keratoderma blennorrhagica (Harrison 22e p.2880).

IBD-associated arthritis: r-axSpA develops in up to 10% of IBD patients and pSpA in 10-30%; conversely axSpA patients have a 5-10% risk of developing IBD. HLA-B27 is NOT a risk factor for IBD itself (Harrison 22e p.2891-2892).
harrison.pathophysiology: SpA is a prototypic chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease that couples inflammation to structural damage, with the unique feature that inflammation-induced bone loss coexists with pathologic new bone formation at specific skeletal sites (sacroiliac joints, anterior spinal ligaments, peripheral entheses). HLA-B27, an MHC class I allele, is the strongest genetic risk factor; proposed mechanisms include the arthritogenic peptide theory (HLA-B27 presenting microbial peptides to CD8+ T cells with molecular mimicry), HLA-B27 homodimerization engaging innate receptors (KIR3DL2) to drive IL-17, and unfolded protein response/autophagy promoting IL-23-driven type 17 immunity. Disease requires additional factors beyond HLA-B27 (only ~5% of HLA-B27-positive people, and 20% of HLA-B27-positive first-degree relatives, develop axSpA); key instigators are loss of intestinal barrier integrity with microbial dysbiosis (germ-free HLA-B27 transgenic rats fail to develop disease) and aberrant response to mechanical stress. The IL-23/IL-17 axis and TNF-alpha are central, with overlapping yet domain-distinct cytokine signatures across gut, joint, entheses, and skin (Harrison 22e p.2880-2882).
additionalDifferentials: Mechanical (nonspecific) back pain - the etiology in 95-96% of chronic back pain; axSpA accounts for only 4-5% (Harrison 22e p.2885)
Fibromyalgia / central sensitization (especially mistaken for SpA in women, delaying diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.2885)

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) - noninflammatory, flowing osteophytes over >=4 contiguous vertebrae, normal sacroiliac joints, in obese diabetic males >50; can be mistaken for bamboo spine (Harrison 22e p.2886)
Osteitis condensans ilii (OCI) - asymptomatic triangular iliac-side sclerosis in multiparous women; lack of erosions distinguishes from axSpA (Harrison 22e p.2886)
Osteoarthritis of the spine - horizontal osteophytes vs vertical syndesmophytes (Harrison 22e p.2884)
Rheumatoid arthritis - symmetric polyarticular MCP/PIP disease, RF/nodules present (Harrison 22e p.2879)
Hypothyroidism and hypovitaminosis D in young patients with generalized body pain (Harrison 22e p.2886)
infectionMimics: Septic sacroiliitis from tuberculosis, brucellosis, fungi, or other infectious agents - can cause inflammatory back pain with sclerotic sacroiliac changes (Harrison 22e p.2886)
Infectious enterocolitis-like acute gut inflammation seen histologically in SpA terminal ileum (Harrison 22e p.2891)
nonInfectiousMimics: Metastatic disease / malignancy, including acute lymphoblastic leukemia presenting with inflammatory back pain and sacroiliac sclerosis (Harrison 22e p.2886)
MRI osteitis-like changes from mechanical stress in athletes, postpartum women, and normal individuals >40 (risk of overdiagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.2885)
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) and gout (may coexist with/mimic PsA) (Harrison 22e p.2889)
SAPHO and hidradenitis suppurativa (may mimic palmoplantar psoriasis/PsA) (Harrison 22e p.2889)
additionalInvestigations: HLA-B27 typing - supportive but neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2884)
ESR and CRP - elevated in only 30-40% of active axSpA; neither sensitive nor specific, but useful for monitoring (Harrison 22e p.2884, 2888)
Plain AP or Ferguson pelvic radiograph for sacroiliitis (multiple oblique views add little and increase gonadal radiation) (Harrison 22e p.2884)

MRI of sacroiliac joints/spine - detects active osteitis/bone marrow edema (STIR) and structural lesions (sclerosis, fat metaplasia, erosions, backfill, ankylosis) early; not indicated for routine monitoring (Harrison 22e p.2885, 2888)
Low-dose CT of sacroiliac joints/spine - emerging alternative to radiography for diagnosis and progression (Harrison 22e p.2885)
Synovial fluid analysis in monoarthritis - WBC >2000/mL with negative crystals/Gram stain/culture suggests inflammatory arthritis; rules out septic and crystal arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2888)
Fecal calprotectin (elevated with microscopic gut inflammation in SpA) (Harrison 22e p.2891)
Disease activity indices: BASDAI, ASDAS; function: BASFI; metrology: BASMI (Harrison 22e p.2886)
redFlags: Fever, weight loss, advanced age, or past malignancy in a back-pain patient - prompt evaluation for osteomyelitis, osteoporotic fracture, or metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.2886)
Cauda equina syndrome (urinary hesitancy and/or saddle anesthesia) - late axSpA complication (Harrison 22e p.2884)
Cardiac conduction abnormalities (heart block) at any stage; aortic valve insufficiency as a late complication (Harrison 22e p.2884)
AA (renal) amyloidosis causing nephrotic syndrome after prolonged uncontrolled inflammation; IgA nephropathy with microscopic hematuria (Harrison 22e p.2884)
Spinal fractures in ankylosed (bamboo) spine - consider if back pain persists/relapses despite therapy (Harrison 22e p.2888)
Atlantoaxial subluxation (rare, in PsA) with potentially serious neurologic consequences (Harrison 22e p.2889)
Acute anterior uveitis (eye pain, redness, photophobia, miosis) requiring urgent ophthalmologic care (Harrison 22e p.2884)
harrison.prognosis: Course is variable: ~50% of patients progress from nonradiographic to radiographic stage over 20 years, but <10% progress to significant spinal involvement with bamboo spine. Risk factors for osteoproliferation (worse structural outcome) include male sex, persistent inflammation (MRI sacroiliac/spine activity, high CRP), existing syndesmophytes, HLA-B27 positivity, and smoking. With increased awareness and earlier treatment, structural damage has steadily decreased over recent decades, with a shift toward higher prevalence of nr-axSpA over r-axSpA. axSpA significantly impairs well-being, function, productivity, and quality of life. Reactive arthritis is often self-limiting but may become chronic, with HLA-B27 linked to chronicity (Harrison 22e p.2880, 2884, 2891).
pitfalls: PITFALL: confusing inflammatory back pain with common mechanical back pain - mechanical causes must be considered first since axSpA is the etiology in only 4-5% of chronic back pain; conversely IBP improves with exercise and worsens with rest, the reverse of mechanical pain (Harrison 22e p.2883, 2885).
The term 'inflammatory back pain' is itself a partial misnomer - only ~15% of patients with IBP have demonstrable axial inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2883).
Diagnostic delay of 5-14 years is common, worse in women (back pain/enthesitis mistaken for fibromyalgia) and in nonwhite populations with lower HLA-B27 prevalence (Harrison 22e p.2884).
Interreader reliability for distinguishing r-axSpA from nr-axSpA on radiographs is poor (kappa 0.35-0.45), even between trained musculoskeletal radiologists (Harrison 22e p.2883).
MRI overdiagnosis: osteitis-type and fat-metaplasia changes occur from mechanical stress in athletes, postpartum women, degenerative arthritis, and normal individuals >40 (Harrison 22e p.2885).
Normal/negative inflammatory markers do NOT exclude axSpA - ESR/CRP elevated in only 30-40% of active disease (Harrison 22e p.2884).
Plain spine radiographs should generally be avoided in chronic back pain; multiple oblique sacroiliac views add little but increase gonadal radiation (Harrison 22e p.2884).

Avoid glucocorticoid injection around lower-extremity weight-bearing entheses due to risk of tendon rupture; in IBD-associated arthritis anti-IL17 therapy is contraindicated and NSAIDs may trigger IBD flares (Harrison 22e p.2890-2892).
harrison.severityClassification: axSpA is classified as radiographic (r-axSpA / ankylosing spondylitis) vs nonradiographic (nr-axSpA) using definitive sacroiliitis on plain radiographs per the modified New York criteria: definitive = grade 2 bilateral OR grade 3-4 unilateral or bilateral (r-axSpA); lower-grade sacroiliitis = nr-axSpA. ASAS criteria further split SpA into axial (axSpA) and peripheral (pSpA). Diagnosis of axSpA in chronic back pain follows the schema of Figure 374-2 (definite sacroiliitis on x-ray -> AS; otherwise count SpA features >=4 or compelling clinical picture plus MRI sacroiliitis/HLA-B27 -> nr-axSpA). Disease activity graded with BASDAI/ASDAS; PsA classified with CASPAR criteria, activity by DAPSA/MDA (Harrison 22e p.2883-2884, 2889).
management: Regular exercise and physiotherapy focused on spinal mobility, posture and function as the cornerstone of non-pharmacological care
NSAIDs as first-line pharmacotherapy for pain and stiffness in axial disease, used continuously where inflammation is persistent
Biologic therapy with TNF-alpha inhibitors or IL-17 inhibitors for active disease inadequately controlled by NSAIDs, with JAK inhibitors as a further option

Conventional synthetic DMARDs such as sulfasalazine or methotrexate for peripheral arthritis, and local corticosteroid injection for enthesitis or monoarthritis, as systemic corticosteroids are of limited value in axial disease
Screen for and manage extra-articular manifestations and comorbidities: uveitis with ophthalmology, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, osteoporosis and cardiovascular risk
Monitor disease activity with composite indices and CRP and track structural progression, adjusting therapy to a treat-to-target approach
Multidisciplinary care with rheumatology and physiotherapy, and orthopaedic or surgical referral for advanced spinal deformity or hip disease
